section_summary: This section combines an OSS study of Japanese press control with postwar correspondence and SCAP statistical reports on newspapers, news services, and publishing. It documents wartime censorship and consolidation, requests for information about the occupied Japanese press, newspaper statistics for March and May 1946, and the opening sixty pages of an extensive directory of current Japanese publishers and their representatives. The publishers directory is heavily concentrated on Tokyo and continues beyond this section.

subfiles.title: The Japanese Press as an Instrument for Control
subfiles.from: Office of Strategic Services, Research and Analysis Branch
subfiles.about: Analyzes the Japanese press as a centralized instrument of wartime social and political control.
subfiles.summary: Study: Japanese papers are influential, widely circulated, efficient and prone to sensationalism; government control uses negative censorship, licensing, confiscation, suspension, penalties and voluntary prepublication review; consolidation, especially Domei, could aid an Allied military government.

subfiles.title: Request for information on the press of occupied Japan
subfiles.from: John R. Price, School of Journalism, Ohio State University
subfiles.to: Department of State, Information and Education Section
subfiles.about: Requests current official material for a comparative study of prewar and postwar Japanese newspapers and publications.
subfiles.summary: Price asks for MacArthur's Press Code, monthly SCAP announcements, current newspaper counts, information on English-language papers, and accounts of production strikes at the Yomiuri Shimbun and Hokkaido Shimbun. He also seeks information on political affiliations, newspaper unions, wartime English-language publishing, and other current reports on the occupied Japanese press.

subfiles.title: Reply forwarding Price's inquiry to the War Department
subfiles.from: Frank W. Schuler Jr., Division of Occupied Areas
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Price's request and forwards it to the War Department's Civil Affairs Division.
subfiles.summary: Schuler tells Price his April 3 request for Japanese press data went to the War Department's Civil Affairs Division, which holds occupied-area material and should reply directly.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about Japanese news services
subfiles.from: Inko Iben, University of Illinois Library
subfiles.to: Hugh Borton, Division of Northeast Asian Affairs
subfiles.about: Asks which Japanese news services should be acquired for scholarly study.
subfiles.summary: Iben wants Japanese news services for scholars, names the Okuyama, Jiji and Kyodo services, and asks whether subscribing to all three duplicates too much.

subfiles.title: Reply on Okuyama, Jiji, and Kyodo services
subfiles.from: John M. Allison, Acting Chief, Division of Northeast Asian Affairs
subfiles.about: Explains the content of three Japanese news services and recommends a combination of subscriptions.
subfiles.summary: Allison says Okuyama translates Japanese editorials and leading articles, while Jiji and Kyodo translate their own staffs' news, so he recommends Okuyama plus either Jiji or Kyodo.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of reports containing Japanese newspaper statistics
subfiles.from: Counselor of Mission, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards SCAP reports on Japanese newspaper statistics and publishers.
subfiles.summary: Despatch sends five copies each of two Civil Information and Education reports on newspapers as of March 15 and May 15, 1946, plus "Current Japanese Publishers."
keywords: United States Political Adviser for Japan

subfiles.title: Routing note on Japanese press and publishing data
subfiles.about: Notes the strengths and limitations of the accompanying Japanese publishing report.
subfiles.summary: Routing note: the report covers the press and publishing business but not circulation or politics, finding 88 percent of Japan's 1,445 firms are in Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Basic Statistics: Newspapers as of 15 March 1946
subfiles.from: Press and Publications Research Unit, Civil Information and Education Section, SCAP
subfiles.about: Tabulates the number, frequency, circulation, employment, distribution, and equipment of Japanese newspapers.
subfiles.summary: Statistics as of March 15, 1946: 418 operating newspapers by type and frequency, 220 ceased or suspended or undetermined; the 55 key dailies have circulation 13,898,506 and 23,221 employees, with prefectural distribution and press equipment.

subfiles.title: Basic Statistics: Newspapers as of 15 May 1946
subfiles.from: Press and Publications Research Unit, Civil Information and Education Section, SCAP
subfiles.about: Classifies Japanese newspapers and news services known to have appeared between March 15 and May 15, 1946.
subfiles.summary: Statistics as of May 15, 1946: 837 publications, 392 general-news and 445 special-interest papers or services by category; the compilers warn of overlap and an incomplete government-publication count.

subfiles.title: Current Japanese Publishers
subfiles.from: Press and Publications Research Unit, Civil Information and Education Section, SCAP
subfiles.about: Provides a geographically arranged directory of Japanese publishers, their addresses, representatives, and publishing specialties.
subfiles.summary: The report is based on lists supplied by the Japanese Publishers Association and Turenami Book Store and estimates that it covers about 90 percent of active publishers. It counts 1,445 firms, including 1,165 in Tokyo, and stresses the extraordinary concentration of publishing and related press activity in the capital. The directory then lists firms alphabetically with addresses, representatives, and codes for books, magazines, or both; this section reaches entries beginning with “Tokyo” and the report continues beyond page 78.
